theme: saying no at work and at home

entries.text: They wrote that their manager asked them to cover the weekend shift again. They said yes even though they had plans, and felt resentful all evening.
Session about saying yes too quickly. They noticed the fear of disappointing people starts in the chest before they even answer. Their therapist suggested pausing for a breath before replying.
Their sister asked them to host the family dinner. They paused, said they could not this time, and did not explain for ten minutes like usual. Felt shaky but proud.
Say no to one request this week
Talked with Orca about the manager asking again. They declined the extra shift, heart pounding, and offered to swap a different day instead.
On the spot in a meeting they were asked to take on a new project. They froze and agreed, then felt stuck. Saying no to the manager in front of others is still really hard.
They told a colleague they could not stay late. Short answer, no long apology. The worry passed faster than before.

theme: Sunday dread and worry about the week

entries.text: Sunday evening again. They noticed the dread about Monday begins around 6 pm, with a tight stomach and racing thoughts about emails.
They described lying awake thinking through every task of the week. Tried writing the worries on paper and it helped them fall asleep a bit sooner.
Talked about worry as a way of trying to control the week. They took away that a thought about Monday is not a fact about Monday.
Wrote down Monday's three hardest tasks on Sunday and closed the notebook. The evening felt calmer than usual.
Wrote the worry list again before bed. Noticed the worries were mostly about what their boss might think.
I worry most when I imagine being judged, not when the work itself is hard.
Sunday was hard but they went for a walk, wrote the list and did not check email. Slept fine.

entries.text: They were furious after their partner forgot the anniversary dinner. They shouted, then regretted it and went silent for a day.
Session on anger. They noticed anger comes when they feel unimportant. Their therapist asked them to try naming the feeling out loud before reacting.
Their partner was late again. They said calmly that they felt unimportant when plans change last minute. The talk went better than shouting ever did.
Argument about chores. They took ten minutes in another room, came back and said what made them angry without blaming. Their partner listened.
Recorded session. They practised saying what they need from the relationship. They noticed they often expect their partner to guess.
They apologised for snapping on Friday and explained what was going on for them. Felt closer afterwards.
